title: Lending, Borrowing, and Interest Rate Curves
objectives: Understand the Money Market Utilization Rate U = Borrows / Deposits
Master the piecewise Kinked Interest Rate Model used by Aave and Kamino
Calculate Supply APY from Borrow APR and protocol reserve factor
Learn why borrowing rates skyrocket during liquidity crunches

steps.title: How Decentralized Money Markets Work
steps.body:
A DeFi money market is a vending machine that never sleeps and never checks your credit. There is no loan officer, no paperwork, and no handshake - just a smart contract and one shared pile of tokens. Depositors drop tokens in to earn yield; borrowers pull tokens out by posting <Term id="collateral">collateral</Term> worth more than the loan. Both sides trade against the very same <Term id="liquidity_pool">liquidity pool</Term>.

**Why this matters before you deposit a single dollar:**

- **Depositors are the suppliers.** You lend your tokens into the pool and earn the interest paid by everyone who borrows from it.
- **Borrowers are the demand.** They overcollateralize (for example, lock $1.50 of SOL to borrow $1.00 of USDC), which is what protects the depositors' funds.
- **Nobody negotiates.** The interest rate is not decided by a committee; it is computed continuously from a single number called the <Term id="utilisation">utilisation</Term> rate.

That one number - utilisation - is the thermostat of the entire market. Turn it up and borrowing gets expensive while lending gets rich; turn it down and the opposite happens. Almost everything else in this lesson is just a consequence of that one dial.

steps.title: The 80% Kink: Why Rates Explode
steps.body:
Utilisation is simply `U = Total Borrows / Total Deposits`. If depositors have supplied $100 and borrowers have taken $80, utilisation is 80%. Now the catch that makes money markets so clever: if utilisation ever reached 100%, there would be literally nothing left for depositors to withdraw. To prevent that quiet bank run before it starts, protocols build a **piecewise kinked interest rate curve** - a rate path with a gentle slope, followed by a terrifying cliff.

**Picture a ski slope that ends at a waterfall:**

- **Below the kink (under ~80%):** Rates climb in a lazy, predictable line. Borrowing is cheap (think 2% to 8% <Term id="apr">APR</Term>), so people happily borrow and depositors still earn a modest, safe yield.
- **At the kink (~80%):** The slope snaps sharply upward. This is the warning line built into the math.
- **Above the kink:** Borrow rates rocket toward 50%-80%+, punishing anyone still borrowing while making fresh deposits wildly attractive.

The genius is that the market self-corrects with no manager in sight. A surge in demand pushes <Term id="utilisation">utilisation</Term> past the kink, which instantly rewards new deposits with a huge <Term id="apy">APY</Term> while squeezing borrowers to repay. Liquidity floods back in long before the <Term id="liquidity_pool">liquidity pool</Term> can be drained dry. The curve *is* the safety mechanism.

steps.title: Under the Hood: The Kink Interest Rate Equation
steps.body:
**Under the hood: the two-slope equation.** Every borrow rate in a money market comes from the same piecewise formula, expressed as <Term id="apr">APR</Term>, where `U_optimal` is the kink point (often 80%).

`If U ≤ U_optimal:  R_borrow = BaseRate + (U / U_optimal) × Slope1`

`If U > U_optimal:  R_borrow = BaseRate + Slope1 + ((U - U_optimal) / (1 - U_optimal)) × Slope2`

**Read it like a market maker:**

- `BaseRate` is the floor borrowers pay even at near-zero utilisation, so supplying is never completely unrewarded.
- `Slope1` is the gentle pre-kink gradient. It rises smoothly with <Term id="utilisation">utilisation</Term>, keeping borrowing attractive while the pool is healthy.
- `Slope2` is the cliff after the kink. It is deliberately steep because it is a liquidity defense, not a pricing strategy - it exists to force repayment fast.
- Depositor <Term id="apy">APY</Term> is then derived from what borrowers actually pay, minus the protocol's cut: `SupplyAPR = U × R_borrow × (1 - ReserveFactor)`.

That last line explains why depositor yield rises with utilisation. The pool only earns interest on the fraction of deposits that is actually borrowed (`U`), and the reserve factor skims a small slice for the protocol and its insurance buffer. Higher utilisation means a bigger share of your deposit is out working - and, past the kink, working at a dramatically higher rate.

questions.prompt: Why do DeFi lending protocols add a steep 'kink' to the interest rate curve above roughly 80% utilisation?
options: To maximise founder profits on every loan issued
Because Solana gas fees scale directly with pool utilisation
To automatically trigger liquidations of every open borrower
To force borrowers to repay and attract new deposits, so the pool is never drained empty
questions.explainRight: Correct. The kink is a liquidity defense, not a profit scheme. Past 80% utilisation the curve spikes, which simultaneously pressures borrowers to repay and tempts new depositors with high <Term id="apy">APY</Term>. That two-sided push keeps the pool solvent and prevents a 100% drain.
questions.explainWrong: The kink is neither about founder profits nor gas fees, and it does not liquidate healthy borrowers. It is a self-correcting safety valve: steep rates above ~80% push borrowers to repay and pull fresh deposits in, refilling the <Term id="liquidity_pool">liquidity pool</Term> before depositors are left unable to withdraw.

questions.prompt: A pool has $1,000,000 in USDC deposits and $400,000 in active borrows. What is the pool's utilisation rate?
questions.explainRight: Correct. <Term id="utilisation">Utilisation</Term> is borrows divided by deposits: $400,000 / $1,000,000 = 40%. That is comfortably below the kink, so borrowing here is still cheap and depositor yield is modest and safe.
questions.explainWrong: Do the division: utilisation equals borrows over deposits, so $400,000 / $1,000,000 = 40%. It cannot exceed 100% because you cannot borrow more than what has been deposited, and 25% would imply only $250,000 borrowed. Always anchor the formula before reading any dashboard.

questions.prompt: If utilisation is 25% and borrowers are paying 10% APR, roughly what supply APR can depositors expect before the reserve factor?
options: About 2.5%, because only the borrowed 25% of deposits is earning interest while the rest sits idle
About 10%, because every depositor earns the full borrow rate regardless of utilisation
About 40%, because the idle 75% is also lent out and earning
About 0%, because supply APY is independent of utilisation
questions.explainRight: Correct. Supply APR is roughly `U × R_borrow`, so 0.25 x 10% ≈ 2.5%. Only the borrowed portion of deposits generates interest, so low utilisation automatically produces lower depositor yield - which is exactly why the kink rewards higher utilisation with richer rates.
questions.explainWrong: Depositors do not earn the full borrow rate, because idle deposits are not lent out. The right approximation is `U × R_borrow` = 0.25 x 10% ≈ 2.5%. Supply yield is deeply dependent on <Term id="utilisation">utilisation</Term>; the more of your deposit that is borrowed, the more of the borrow interest flows to you.

questions.prompt: Suppose utilisation climbs from 60% to 92% in a pool with an 80% kink. What happens to the borrow rate, and why?
options: It stays flat, because the base rate floors the curve at every level
It falls, because more borrowers spread the cost across the pool
It jumps sharply, because the pool has crossed the kink and the steep Slope2 now applies
It is unaffected until utilisation hits exactly 100%
questions.explainRight: Correct. Below 80% the rate follows the gentle Slope1 line, but 92% is past the kink, so Slope2 kicks in and the <Term id="apr">APR</Term> shoots upward. That violent jump is the whole point: it makes borrowing painful and depositing lucrative right when the pool most needs help.
questions.explainWrong: The rate does not stay flat, fall, or wait for 100%. Crossing the 80% kink switches the formula to the much steeper Slope2 segment, so the borrow APR spikes. That is how the curve defends the <Term id="liquidity_pool">liquidity pool</Term>: it prices the last drops of liquidity very, very expensively.

questions.prompt: Two depositors supply identical amounts. Pool A runs at 20% utilisation and Pool B at 85%. Assuming similar base rates, why does Pool B pay much more?
options: Higher utilisation means more of every deposit is lent out, and being past the kink applies a dramatically higher interest rate to that borrowed capital
Pool B pays more because it charges depositors a fee to withdraw their money
Pool B mints extra reward tokens to inflate its advertised yield
Pool A pays more, since idle liquidity is safer and therefore yields more
questions.explainRight: Correct. Two effects stack in Pool B's favor: a larger share of deposits (85% vs 20%) is actively earning, and being past the 80% kink means that borrowed capital is charged a much higher rate. Depositor yield rises on both counts - more capital working, at a richer rate.
questions.explainWrong: Pool B does not charge withdrawal fees or mint fake rewards, and higher utilisation, not idle liquidity, drives yield. The real explanation is combination: more of the deposit is lent out *and* the kink pushes the borrow <Term id="apr">APR</Term> higher. Supply yield scales with utilisation and with the rate that utilisation triggers.

questions.prompt: A whale deposits a huge amount of USDC into a pool sitting at 90% utilisation. All else equal, what is the most likely near-term effect?
options: Utilisation stays at 90% and the new deposit earns the old, elevated rate
The whale's deposit instantly pushes the pool past the kink toward 100%
Deposits do not affect utilisation, so nothing changes
Utilisation falls (more deposits, same borrows), which lowers the borrow rate and the whale's own yield - rewarding early exit for the existing lenders
questions.explainRight: Exactly. Utilisation is borrows over deposits, so a large deposit raises the denominator and pushes U down. Coming back below the kink collapses the borrow rate, which lowers the very yield the whale came for. This is the self-correcting logic in reverse: liquidity arriving at a crunch automatically dilutes the rich rate.
questions.explainWrong: Adding deposits cannot push utilisation toward 100% - it moves it the other way. More deposits with the same borrows means U falls, which eases the rate back down below the kink. The subtle lesson is that the high yield at a crunch is a signal to supply liquidity, and supplying it is precisely what erases the premium.

questions.prompt: Borrow demand suddenly surges, pushing a healthy pool from 50% to 95% utilisation. Which description best captures how the protocol self-heals?
options: Borrowers pay a fixed rate, so the pool relies on an administrator to add liquidity manually
The kinked rate spikes borrowing costs, forcing repayment, while boosting supply APY, attracting fresh deposits - pulling utilisation back below the kink with no manager involved
The protocol pauses all withdrawals until utilisation returns to 50%
High utilisation automatically liquidates every borrower to refill the pool
questions.explainRight: Correct. The kink works both sides at once: borrowers face punishing rates that make repaying rational, and depositors see a huge <Term id="apy">APY</Term> that pulls in new capital. Borrows fall and deposits rise, so utilisation naturally retreats below the kink - no admin, no pause, no forced liquidations required.
questions.explainWrong: There is no administrator, no withdrawal freeze, and no blanket liquidation of healthy loans. The curve heals itself by pricing the crunch: high borrow cost drives repayment while high supply yield attracts deposits, so both sides of the <Term id="utilisation">utilisation</Term> ratio move in the right direction at the same time.
